answer_text: {"verdict": "mixed", "reason": "Knocking out the receptor in the blood-exposed area postrema blunted the aversive response to a circulating appetite drug, which fits the test's idea that blocking direct blood-to-nerve chemical access dulls a sickly bodily state. However, the passages report no role for those neurons in normal physiological feeding (involving the body's own chemistry), and because the blood-brain barrier keeps the circulating drug from reaching neighbouring brainstem neurons, removing the area postrema receptor may just block an external drug's entry point rather than showing that nerve-to-nerve signalling alone cannot produce feelings. Because of this, the given passages cannot tell Damasio's prediction apart from a purely neural account once a signal enters the brain. Beyond the material given, this reading relies only on standard expansions of the passages' abbreviations (AP = area postrema, NTS = nucleus of the solitary tract, BBB = blood-brain barrier, GLP1RA/Lira = GLP-1 receptor agonist/liraglutide, KO = knockout, CTA = conditioned taste aversion in mice).", "unsure": true, "unsure_why": "Evidence from the study or elsewhere showing whether ordinary nerve-to-nerve activation of this brainstem circuit still produces (against) or fails to produce (for) the aversive state when direct blood-to-nerve chemical exchange is blocked, and whether endogenous bodily feelings rather than just exogenous drug responses are dulled, would change the verdict."}
